title: Seating Arrangements & Puzzles
relevance: Banking/placement OAs and reasoning screens use seating, floor, and schedule puzzles to test constraint tracking and systematic elimination under time pressure.

phases.goal: Establish the universal solve order and facing-direction conventions before placing anyone.

must_hit.point: Sketch the row, circle, or grid frame before reading all the clues.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says draw the structure first, then drop clues into it.

must_hit.point: Place the most constrained clue first: definitive statements before relative ones.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions starting with fixed ends or exact positions, not 'somewhere left of'.

must_hit.point: Facing centre means left is clockwise; facing outward means left is counter-clockwise.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both centre and outward left directions correctly without using their own left/right.

must_hit.point: In linear arrangements, North-facing left is your left; South-facing left is your right.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly flips left/right when a person or row faces South.

probes: Walk me through the first things you do when you open a seating puzzle, before placing names.
How does 'left' change when someone faces the centre versus outward?

hints.1: Think about what you put on paper before chasing every clue.
hints.2: Order of attack: frame, then absolute placements, then relative ones; facing sets left/right.
hints.3: Draw the frame first; start with definitive clues; centre→left clockwise, outward→left counter-clockwise; North left=your left, South left=your right.

phases.goal: Show how linear, parallel-row, and circular constraints are placed and how invalid cases are eliminated.

must_hit.point: In a single-row linear arrangement, unless stated otherwise, assume everyone faces North.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the default North-facing assumption for a single row.

must_hit.point: In a two-row arrangement, one row faces North and the other faces South, so the South-facing row has left/right reversed from our view.
must_hit.evidence_hint: For parallel rows, correctly reverses left for the South-facing row when placing 'second to the left'.

must_hit.point: When seats are numbered anti-clockwise and people face the centre, moving 'right' follows the anti-clockwise numbering.
must_hit.evidence_hint: In a centre-facing circle, places someone third/second to the right by moving anti-clockwise along the numbering.

must_hit.point: When multiple layouts are possible, keep cases and discard any that contradict a later neighbour or facing clue.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes branching cases then killing one when a neighbour-facing clue fails.

probes: In two parallel rows facing each other, how do you interpret 'R sits second to the left of the person who faces A'?
If eight people face the centre around a circle and seats are numbered anti-clockwise, which way is 'to the right'?

hints.1: Separate single-row defaults from two-row facing.
hints.2: South-facing left is flipped; centre-facing right follows anti-clockwise numbering; keep cases until a clue breaks one.
hints.3: Single row defaults North; two-row South row reverses left; centre-facing right = anti-clockwise on anti-clockwise seats; eliminate contradicting cases.

phases.goal: Contrast clue-ordering and facing conventions that change how left/right are applied.

must_hit.point: Prefer definitive placements (extreme end, fixed seat) over relative placements early, because relative clues leave too many open positions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Argues starting with extreme-end or fixed-position clues to shrink possibilities.

must_hit.point: Choosing centre-facing versus outward-facing flips which way 'left' and 'right' run around the circle.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains that the same verbal left/right maps opposite ways depending on facing.

must_hit.point: Do not map your own left and right onto top/bottom seats without flipping by each person's facing direction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns against egocentric left/right on circle seats and insists on per-person facing.

probes: Why start with 'A sits at the extreme right end' before 'B is somewhere left of C'?
What goes wrong if you treat every circle seat's left as your left while drawing?

hints.1: Compare absolute clues to vague relative ones.
hints.2: Facing direction is the switch that flips clockwise vs counter-clockwise left.
hints.3: Definitive clues first; centre left=clockwise, outward left=counter-clockwise; never paste your own left onto seats without facing flip.

phases.goal: Apply the same constraint method to matrix/floor, weekday schedule, and OA-disguised desk puzzles.

must_hit.point: Modern OAs often disguise standard linear or matrix puzzles as corporate team or server-rack stories; extract pure constraints onto a scratchpad immediately.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Strips story framing and restates only seating/attribute constraints.

must_hit.point: Floor/matrix puzzles are solved on a grid of floors, people, and attributes by eliminating impossible floors from odd/even and 'immediately above/below' clues.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Builds a floor×person×attribute table and uses odd-floor / immediately-above constraints to force placements.

must_hit.point: Weekday scheduling uses consecutive-pair slots and fixed-day anchors, then fits gap constraints into the remaining days.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Pins the fixed day, lists legal consecutive pairs, then places the two-day-gap pair in leftover slots.

probes: An OA describes five engineers at adjacent desks with end, gap, and immediate-neighbour clues—how do you start?
How would you set up a five-floor puzzle where each person also has a different car?

hints.1: Ignore the corporate wrapping; treat it as a normal lineup.
hints.2: For floors, draw a grid; for schedules, lock fixed days and legal consecutive pairs first.
hints.3: Translate OA story→linear constraints; floors→people/attribute grid with above/below elimination; schedule→fixed day + consecutive + gap fit.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Start with definitive statements such as sitting at an extreme end; relative clues like 'somewhere left of' leave too many open seats until the frame is constrained.
Facing centre: left is clockwise. Facing outward: left is counter-clockwise. The same 'left/right' words reverse around the table when facing flips.

tradeoffs.topic: Drawing the frame first vs reading all clues first
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Sketch the row, circle, or grid before reading all clues so each placement has a structure to drop into rather than holding unbound verbal constraints in memory.

gotchas.trap: Mapping your own left and right onto top/bottom circle seats without flipping for facing direction.
gotchas.correction: When facing the centre, left is clockwise; when facing outward, left is counter-clockwise—always flip by the person's facing, not yours.

gotchas.trap: Treating OA 'corporate team assignment' or 'server rack placement' wording as reading comprehension.
gotchas.correction: The underlying logic is still a standard linear or matrix puzzle; extract the pure constraints onto a scratchpad immediately.

gotchas.trap: In parallel rows, applying North-facing left/right to the South-facing row.
gotchas.correction: The South-facing row has left/right reversed from our perspective; 'second to the left' for that row is our right.
